Mip-mapping for style functions is a technique to avoid aliasing in style lookups while preventing mixing between styles at higher mip-map levels [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that mip-mapping is used to avoid aliasing in texture mapping (style lookups). It further explains that for 3D textures, standard mip-mapping causes 'undesired mixing between styles' at higher levels, and that the authors perform 'custom mip-map generation to avoid mixing between styles at their borders.' This directly supports the claim that the technique avoids aliasing while preventing style mixing.

The claim lists three specific limitations: 1) Requires manual mip-map level computation, 2) undefined hardware derivatives in loops, and 3) potential artifacts in high-curvature areas. The evidence explicitly states that hardware derivatives are undefined in conditionals or loops (like raycasting), necessitating manual computation of the projected voxel size.
